Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Vocabulary: comparable sale: A completed sale selected for its relevance to a property's pricing analysis. / comparative market analysis: An agent's comparison of relevant market evidence for a pricing discussion. / subject property: The property being evaluated or discussed. / sale price: The reported amount paid in a completed transaction. / list price: The advertised asking amount for a property. / price reduction: A decrease in the advertised asking amount. / days on market: A listing-duration measure under a stated counting method. / absorption rate: A sales-to-inventory measure over a specified period and definition. / months of supply: Inventory divided by a defined monthly sales pace. / concession: A negotiated benefit or contribution affecting transaction terms. / adjustment: A supported modification used to account for a relevant difference. / condition: The physical state of a property or component. / renovation: Work altering or improving an existing property. / deferred maintenance: Upkeep that has been postponed and may require attention. / living area: Space included under a stated residential measurement definition. / lot size: The measured area of the parcel of land. / measurement source: The record or method from which a size figure comes. / price per square foot: Price divided by area under a specified measurement basis. / market exposure: The extent and duration of a property's availability to prospective buyers. / arm's-length transaction: A transaction between independent parties acting in their own interests. / listing status: The current recorded stage of a property listing. / pending sale: A transaction under contract but not yet completed under the local usage. / valuation date: The date for which a value opinion is expressed. / pricing range: A proposed interval for pricing discussion based on specified evidence.
Speaking task: Check the answers and read the price discussion in pairs. Say $470,000, $540,000, and $430,000 distinctly; correct forty-three thousand to forty thousand. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Stress unadjusted mean and measurement source. Keep $480,000 as arithmetic, not an appraisal or supported adjustment. Complete the pending-sale exchange, check the key, and reread it. Keep the $520,000 asking price separate from an unreported completed sale price.
Partner: Rosa: Seller / Dev: Listing agent
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A property was listed at $520,000 and is now pending. Its final sale price has not been reported. A presentation labels $520,000 as the confirmed closed price.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Rosa: Could your recommendation include a range and explain why A gets more attention? I want to follow the reasoning.
Dev: Yes. A pricing range lets us explain the evidence and limits. It will not promise what a buyer offers or an appraiser concludes.
Rosa: Keep the three sales, then. Before we choose the asking figure, check the areas, concessions, and other important differences.
Dev: I will also verify each record's listing status. Closed prices, pending transactions, and active asking prices should not be presented as equivalent evidence.
END REFERENCE
04Showings, Open Houses, Fair Housing, and AdvertisingDescribe the home, not the preferred household+

Your goal

Revise exclusionary listing language and handle showing questions with consistent, property-focused information.

This lesson in the book, page 31 ↗

A Read the situation

Describe the home, not the preferred household

A draft listing describes a home as "perfect for couples without children." The verified property facts are two bedrooms, a fenced patio, and a park 0.4 miles away. No bedroom-size measurements or step-free route details have been confirmed. Listing coordinator Fern and open-house host Malik must replace the household preference with factual copy before review. The viewing team is to provide the same property information and apply the same stated booking process to all visitors, while routing access-related requests for appropriate handling.

Fern: Listing coordinator / Malik: Open-house host

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. Which draft wording creates the central concern?

Answer and explanation

C. Perfect for couples without children

The household preference describes favored occupants rather than the supplied property features and requires correction.

2. Which facts are verified in the case?

Answer and explanation

A. Two bedrooms, a fenced patio, and the park distance

Only the room count, patio feature, and park distance are supplied as verified property facts.

3. What is the required viewing approach?

Answer and explanation

B. Consistent property information and booking process, with appropriate handling of access requests

The briefing requires consistent service and routing access-related requests, not invented restrictions or intrusive assumptions.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

A property description should not become a statement about the preferred buyer's family status. The supplied wording needs correction; replacing it with verified room count, outdoor space, and distance information preserves useful marketing content without choosing the occupants.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
fair housing
Equal housing opportunity under applicable nondiscrimination requirements.follow fair-housing requirements
protected characteristic
A trait covered by an applicable nondiscrimination law.avoid decisions based on protected characteristics
familial status
A protected housing category concerning children and related circumstances under US federal law.recognize familial-status concerns
steering
Directing housing choices on a prohibited discriminatory basis.avoid discriminatory steering
discriminatory preference
Wording or conduct favoring or excluding a protected group.remove a discriminatory preference
equal service
Consistent access to relevant assistance under applicable requirements.provide equal service
objective feature
A property characteristic that can be described and checked.describe objective features
occupancy standard
A rule about permitted occupancy requiring legal and factual context.verify an occupancy standard
reasonable accommodation
A disability-related change to a rule, policy, practice, or service where required.route a reasonable-accommodation request
reasonable modification
A disability-related physical change to premises where protected or required.distinguish a reasonable modification
access request
A request concerning how someone can enter, view, or use a property.respond to an access request
showing appointment
An arranged property-viewing time.confirm a showing appointment
open house
A scheduled period when a property is available for visits.host an open house
visitor register
A record of attendees collected under a stated process.maintain the visitor register
booking process
The steps used to arrange a visit.apply a consistent booking process
availability statement
Information about whether and when a property can be viewed or obtained.verify the availability statement
property amenity
A useful feature or facility associated with a property.describe property amenities
fenced patio
An outdoor paved area enclosed by fencing.verify the fenced patio
advertising copy
Written language used to market a property.review advertising copy
photograph caption
Text explaining what a property image shows.check the photograph caption
virtual tour
A digital presentation allowing a remote view of a property.offer the approved virtual tour
disclosure packet
A collected set of required or relevant property disclosures.provide the disclosure packet
showing feedback
Information returned after a property visit.record property-focused showing feedback
complaint route
The process for raising and handling a service concern.explain the complaint route

Consistent service does not mean ignoring an access-related request. Obtain the relevant practical details and route the request under the applicable process. Do not invent a universal occupancy limit, certify an unverified access route, or demand unnecessary medical information as casual conversation.

C Notice the language

A welcoming description need not select the occupants

Promotional wording can communicate an exclusion even when its writer intends warmth. Keep the conversation focused on the property and consistent service. An access question deserves precise information and appropriate handling, not assumptions about someone's medical history or whether they belong in the home.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Identify the concern
This line expresses a household preference rather than a property feature.
Offer factual copy
The home has two bedrooms, a fenced patio, and a park 0.4 miles away.
Keep the review
The revised advertisement still needs the appropriate review.
Apply consistency
Give every visitor the same relevant property information.
Avoid steering
Let visitors assess the property against their own stated needs.
Verify availability
Do not change the availability story based on who is asking.
Handle access precisely
Which route or viewing arrangement would you like us to check?
Close with ownership
I will send the request to the responsible colleague and track the response.
Avoid a diagnosis
We need the practical access information, not an unnecessary medical history.
Mark unverified details
Bedroom measurements and the step-free route are not yet confirmed.
Check the image
The photograph should not imply a feature we have not verified.
Correct the copies
Replace the wording in every version using the same approved text.
Separate room count
Two bedrooms does not itself establish a universal occupancy rule.
Respect the question
I can confirm the features we know and obtain the missing details.
Record useful feedback
Note the visitor's property questions without guessing personal suitability.
Escalate a concern
Use the complaint route if someone reports inconsistent treatment.
6 language and precision notes
Property versus occupants
Keep the subject of the advertisement on the home and its verified features.
Perfect for
This phrase may imply a preferred household when followed by personal characteristics.
Same relevant information
Consistency concerns the quality and availability of service, not ignoring individual access needs.
Not yet confirmed
Use this for measurements or access details that have not been checked.
Which arrangement
A practical question focuses on the request instead of demanding unrelated personal details.
Needs review
Identifying a concern is not the same as giving final legal clearance to revised copy.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which revision best uses the supplied facts?

Answer and explanation

B. Two bedrooms, a fenced patio, and a park 0.4 miles away.

The bedroom, patio, and distance description uses verified property facts instead of a household preference or an unverified access claim.

2. Which reply handles an access question appropriately?

Answer and explanation

A. Tell me which route or arrangement to check, and I will route the request.

The reply seeks practical details and appropriate handling without making unsupported assumptions or demanding irrelevant information.

3. Which revised listing adds no unsupported feature or household preference?

Answer and explanation

A. Two bedrooms, a fenced patio, and a park 0.4 miles away.

Only the bedroom count, patio, and park distance are verified. Spaciousness, doorway clearances, and step-free access need evidence; the child-free description retains the household preference.

4. Which conduct violates the supplied service approach?

Answer and explanation

B. Claiming different availability because of a visitor's perceived household type

The briefing requires consistent availability information and booking processes rather than demographic assumptions.

  18. Malik

  19. Fern
    I will change all three versions: website, printed sheet, and host notes. Please check that the team uses the revised copy at the viewing.
  20. Malik

Answers and explanations
  1. discriminatory preference Turn 2. The wording favors a household without children rather than describing the property, creating a familial-status concern.
  2. objective feature Turn 4. An objective feature describes something about the property that can be checked, rather than a favored type of occupant.
  3. advertising copy Turn 6. Advertising copy communicates to potential buyers; the message it conveys matters even if the writer describes a different intention.
  4. steering Turn 8. Steering directs housing choices on an improper discriminatory basis; visitors should assess objective facts against their own needs.
  5. disclosure packet Turn 10. The shared property-information packet should preserve what is known and what still needs verification, rather than create unsupported assurances.
  6. access request Turn 12. An access request needs practical route or arrangement information; the case does not establish that the route is already suitable.
  7. reasonable accommodation Turn 14. A reasonable-accommodation request concerns a disability-related change to a rule or service and should receive appropriate handling under applicable requirements.
  8. booking process Turn 16. The booking process should be applied consistently rather than altered because of assumptions about a visitor's household.
  9. showing feedback Turn 18. Showing feedback should capture property-related observations and questions, not invented judgments about a visitor's personal suitability.
  10. complaint route Turn 20. The complaint route gives visitors and staff a defined way to raise concerns about service or treatment.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Requesting a property-focused description

The lesson's listing draft describes an ideal type of family rather than the property; specific replacement features have not been supplied.

  1. Broker: Could you revise the listing so it describes the property rather than an ideal type of family?
  2. Listing writer: What kind of replacement would preserve useful information without guessing who should live there?
  3. Broker: Use verified property features, and request missing details instead of substituting assumptions about prospective occupants.
  4. Listing writer: Should I invent a spacious-garden claim because that sounds less personal?
  5. Broker: No. We haven't established that feature. Property-focused wording still needs factual support.
  6. Listing writer: I'll ask for confirmed layout and amenity details before proposing the revised description.
  7. Broker: Good. Our review should also consider the applicable advertising requirements without relying on stereotypes or steering.
  8. Listing writer: Can you confirm the review route before we schedule publication of the revision?
  9. Broker: I'll arrange that check. I can't call the revised advertisement approved before it's assessed.
  10. Listing writer: Then I'll provide a factual draft for review, with any missing material fact identified.
A showing request needs a route check

Separate fictional showing: a visitor requests a step-free route; the agent has not verified access to the property entrance.

  1. Showing agent: Could you confirm whether there is a step-free route to the entrance before I finalize this showing?
  2. Property coordinator: I haven't checked the route. Is the visitor asking us to assume the building is fully accessible?
  3. Showing agent: No. The request concerns the entrance route, and we should clarify that specific feature.
  4. Property coordinator: I'll ask the responsible property contact rather than infer access from the front photograph.
  5. Showing agent: Please confirm a realistic time for the check, since the appointment shouldn't imply verified access.
  6. Property coordinator: Would a reasonable-accommodation question require a separate review if the existing route doesn't meet the request?
  7. Showing agent: We should route that appropriately under the actual circumstances, not invent a universal rule here.
  8. Property coordinator: I'll return the verified route information and identify anything that still needs assessment.
  9. Showing agent: Thank you. I'll keep the visitor updated without promising a feature that hasn't been checked.
  10. Property coordinator: The next action is the route check, with appointment details to be confirmed afterward.
Rejecting a request to screen by imagined residents

Separate fictional open-house planning: a seller asks the agent to invite only people who seem like the current neighbors; no legitimate property-related criterion is given.

  1. Seller: Could you invite only buyers who seem like the current neighbors to the open house?
  2. Listing agent: Please focus any request on the property and the showing arrangements, not assumptions about who belongs here.
  3. Seller: I meant people who would fit in. Can you turn that into a screening description?
  4. Listing agent: I can't use that vague idea to sort visitors by personal characteristics or implied protected-class preferences.
  5. Seller: Then what information can we usefully confirm before the event?
  6. Listing agent: The actual viewing arrangements and verified property details, with any advertising concern referred for review.
  7. Seller: Could you request those details from the property coordinator and leave resident descriptions out?
  8. Listing agent: Yes. I'll keep the invitation property-focused and avoid steering people based on an imagined community fit.
  9. Seller: I understand. My request should concern the event, not the type of person who attends.
  10. Listing agent: Good. We'll review the factual invitation through the proper process before it is distributed.

4. Repeat with three new exchanges, one at a time, moving from recognition to a more subtle meaning contrast. Do not copy the published checks. Label invented variations and do not turn uncertainty into a promise.
5. End with a short contrast table and two supported spoken turns using supplied frames. Accept accurate alternatives in oral practice; acknowledge and replace ambiguous multiple-choice items.

Lesson 04: Showings, Open Houses, Fair Housing, and Advertising
Original fictional case: A draft listing describes a home as "perfect for couples without children." The verified property facts are two bedrooms, a fenced patio, and a park 0.4 miles away. No bedroom-size measurements or step-free route details have been confirmed. Listing coordinator Fern and open-house host Malik must replace the household preference with factual copy before review. The viewing team is to provide the same property information and apply the same stated booking process to all visitors, while routing access-related requests for appropriate handling.
Language workshop: Describe the home, not the preferred household
Communication goal: Revise exclusionary listing language and handle showing questions with consistent, property-focused information.
Language guidance: A property description should not become a statement about the preferred buyer's family status. The supplied wording needs correction; replacing it with verified room count, outdoor space, and distance information preserves useful marketing content without choosing the occupants.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): This line expresses a household preference rather than a property feature. / The home has two bedrooms, a fenced patio, and a park 0.4 miles away. / The revised advertisement still needs the appropriate review. / Give every visitor the same relevant property information. / Let visitors assess the property against their own stated needs. / Do not change the availability story based on who is asking. / Which route or viewing arrangement would you like us to check? / I will send the request to the responsible colleague and track the response. / We need the practical access information, not an unnecessary medical history. / Bedroom measurements and the step-free route are not yet confirmed. / The photograph should not imply a feature we have not verified. / Replace the wording in every version using the same approved text. / Two bedrooms does not itself establish a universal occupancy rule. / I can confirm the features we know and obtain the missing details. / Note the visitor's property questions without guessing personal suitability. / Use the complaint route if someone reports inconsistent treatment.
Vocabulary: fair housing: Equal housing opportunity under applicable nondiscrimination requirements. / protected characteristic: A trait covered by an applicable nondiscrimination law. / familial status: A protected housing category concerning children and related circumstances under US federal law. / steering: Directing housing choices on a prohibited discriminatory basis. / discriminatory preference: Wording or conduct favoring or excluding a protected group. / equal service: Consistent access to relevant assistance under applicable requirements. / objective feature: A property characteristic that can be described and checked. / occupancy standard: A rule about permitted occupancy requiring legal and factual context. / reasonable accommodation: A disability-related change to a rule, policy, practice, or service where required. / reasonable modification: A disability-related physical change to premises where protected or required. / access request: A request concerning how someone can enter, view, or use a property. / showing appointment: An arranged property-viewing time. / open house: A scheduled period when a property is available for visits. / visitor register: A record of attendees collected under a stated process. / booking process: The steps used to arrange a visit. / availability statement: Information about whether and when a property can be viewed or obtained. / property amenity: A useful feature or facility associated with a property. / fenced patio: An outdoor paved area enclosed by fencing. / advertising copy: Written language used to market a property. / photograph caption: Text explaining what a property image shows. / virtual tour: A digital presentation allowing a remote view of a property. / disclosure packet: A collected set of required or relevant property disclosures. / showing feedback: Information returned after a property visit. / complaint route: The process for raising and handling a service concern.

Keep consistency in information separate from refusing to handle an access-related request. Complete and check the doorway exchange. Partner: Fern: Listing coordinator / Malik: Open-house host

05Offers, Counteroffers, Negotiation, and ContingenciesA thirty-day offer with an unconfirmed loan timeline+

Your goal

Discuss offer timing and protections without turning a proposal or lender estimate into a binding assurance.

This lesson in the book, page 40 ↗

A Read the situation

A thirty-day offer with an unconfirmed loan timeline

Buyer Tomas wants to propose a $420,000 purchase, an $8,000 earnest-money deposit, and closing in 30 days. The lender has given only a provisional 35-45-day processing estimate, not final approval. No offer has been submitted or accepted. Agent Elise must explain the timing mismatch and review the proposed financing contingency and deposit terms with the appropriate professionals. The buyer has not authorized removing any protection, and no seller concession or extension has been agreed.

Tomas: Buyer / Elise: Buyer's agent

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What timing mismatch is stated?

Answer and explanation

B. A 30-day proposed close versus a provisional 35-45-day lender estimate

The buyer's proposed date is earlier than the lender's provisional range, and neither establishes final financing approval.

2. What is the current offer status?

Answer and explanation

C. Not submitted or accepted

The briefing explicitly says no offer has been submitted or accepted.

3. What has Tomas not authorized?

Answer and explanation

D. Removing any protection

The case permits discussion but contains no instruction to remove protections.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Proposed closing in 30 days is not the same as a lender confirming that financing can be ready then. An estimate of 35-45 days creates a specific issue to resolve. Avoid describing either the proposed date or the provisional estimate as a guarantee.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
purchase offer
Proposed terms for buying a property.prepare a purchase offer
counteroffer
A response proposing different terms instead of accepting the original offer.review a counteroffer
acceptance
Agreement to an offer under the applicable legal requirements.confirm valid acceptance
offer expiration
The point when an offer ceases to remain open under its terms.verify the offer expiration
earnest money
A deposit showing commitment, governed by the contract and applicable rules.explain earnest-money terms
deposit holder
The authorized person or entity holding a transaction deposit.identify the deposit holder
contingency
A contractual condition affecting obligations or available rights.review the contingency
financing contingency
A contract condition addressing financing under specified terms.explain the financing contingency
inspection contingency
A contract condition addressing inspection and related rights.review the inspection contingency
appraisal contingency
A contract condition addressing appraised value and related rights.clarify the appraisal contingency
home-sale contingency
A condition connected to selling another property.review the home-sale contingency
contingency deadline
The contractual time limit for a condition or related action.track the contingency deadline
waiver
Giving up a right or condition under applicable requirements.explain the proposed waiver
amendment
An agreed change to an existing agreement.document an amendment
addendum
Additional document or terms incorporated into an agreement.review the addendum
seller credit
A seller contribution toward specified buyer costs under permitted terms.request a seller credit
possession date
The date the buyer is entitled to take possession under the agreement.confirm the possession date
closing date
The scheduled or agreed date for completing closing steps.verify the closing date
extension request
A proposal to move an existing deadline.submit an extension request
notice requirement
Rules governing how and when a contractual notice must be given.check the notice requirement
default
Failure to meet a contractual obligation as defined by the agreement and law.obtain advice about default
remedy
A response or relief available under an agreement or law.clarify available remedies
authorized instruction
A direction given by someone with the relevant decision-making authority.record the authorized instruction
negotiating position
The terms and priorities a party is prepared to advance.clarify the negotiating position

A contingency has exact conditions, deadlines, and notice requirements; its name alone does not explain every protection. Deposit recovery is not automatically assured by calling money earnest money. Actual rights need the contract and qualified advice, especially before waiver or amendment.

C Notice the language

Separate a stronger offer from an uninformed promise

A buyer may want to appear decisive in a competitive negotiation. Help them distinguish an attractive term from a term they can reasonably support. Keep the client's authority central and explain the review needed before changing conditions, rather than treating urgency as permission to remove protections.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Name the mismatch
The proposed 30-day close is earlier than the lender's provisional range.
Keep status clear
No offer has been submitted or accepted yet.
Check feasibility
Let us ask the lender what supports the current timing estimate.
Preserve authority
I will not remove a protection without your informed instruction and proper review.
Explain the condition
We need to read the financing contingency's exact terms.
Avoid a refund promise
The deposit's treatment depends on the contract and applicable requirements.
Separate request and agreement
Asking for an extension does not mean the seller has agreed.
Close with review
Confirm the timing and terms before authorizing the offer.
State the price
Your proposed purchase price is $420,000.
Clarify the deposit
The proposed earnest-money amount is $8,000.
Check the notice
Who must receive the notice, by what method, and by when?
Separate possession
Closing and possession dates should not be assumed identical.
Record priorities
Which terms are you authorizing us to propose?
Avoid pressure language
Urgency does not remove the need to understand the consequences.
Review a counter
A counteroffer changes the proposed terms and requires a decision.
Confirm the final version
Use the exact version you have reviewed and authorized.
6 language and precision notes
Propose versus promise
A proposed term is a negotiating position; a promise can create a stronger assurance.
Subject to financing
The phrase is incomplete without the actual contractual condition and required actions.
Requested versus agreed
An extension request does not alter a deadline by itself.
May be refundable
Any statement about deposit return needs the governing terms and facts.
Authorize versus discuss
Exploring an option is not an instruction to submit it.
By when and how
Contractual notices can depend on both timing and delivery requirements.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which sentence handles the timing accurately?

Answer and explanation

C. We need to resolve the gap between the proposed 30 days and the lender's provisional 35-45 days.

The sentence retains both actual timeframes and their status without inventing approval or agreement.

2. Which statement about the deposit is appropriate?

Answer and explanation

D. We need the exact contract terms before explaining when the deposit could be returned.

The deposit's treatment depends on the agreement, applicable rules, and facts rather than its label or amount alone.

3. What should Elise do before removing a protection?

Answer and explanation

A. Obtain informed client instruction and the necessary review of consequences.

The case contains no authorization to remove protections; urgency is not a substitute for an informed decision.

4. The buyer has requested more time, but no acceptance is supplied. Which update is accurate?

Answer and explanation

C. The extension is requested; agreement to change the deadline is unconfirmed.

Delivery of a request proves neither acceptance nor suspension of a deadline. A lender's processing estimate also cannot by itself amend the parties' terms.

Check explanations in the book, page 93 ↗

E Conversations

A thirty-day offer with an unconfirmed loan timeline

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Tomas: Buyer / Elise: Buyer's agent

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank

  • deposit holder

  1. Tomas
    I want to offer four hundred twenty thousand dollars, with eight thousand in earnest money and a thirty-day close. That should look decisive.
  2. Elise
    We can discuss those terms, but the proposed 1 conflicts with the lender's current thirty-five-to-forty-five-day estimate. We need to resolve that gap before presenting thirty days as feasible.
  3. Tomas

  4. Elise

  5. Tomas

  6. Elise

  7. Tomas

  8. Elise

  9. Tomas

  10. Elise

  14. Elise

  15. Tomas

  16. Elise

Answers and explanations
  1. closing date Turn 2. The proposed closing date is earlier than the lender's provisional processing range and is not yet an agreed or assured date.
  2. financing contingency Turn 4. The financing contingency has specific contractual conditions and actions; it cannot turn an unconfirmed timeline into guaranteed financing.
  3. waiver Turn 6. A waiver gives up a right or condition; discussing competitiveness does not authorize the agent to remove protections.
  4. earnest money Turn 8. Earnest money is governed by the agreement and applicable requirements; the label does not guarantee automatic return.
  5. contingency deadline Turn 10. A contingency deadline governs timely exercise or satisfaction of a condition; its consequences depend on the actual contract.
  6. extension request Turn 12. An extension request proposes a new deadline; it does not change the existing agreement without the required acceptance.
  7. counteroffer Turn 14. A counteroffer proposes different terms and requires review; it should not be reported as acceptance of the unchanged original offer.
  8. deposit holder Turn 16. The deposit holder is the person or entity authorized to hold the funds; the case has not yet established that arrangement.
  9. possession date Turn 18. Possession is governed by the agreement and need not be identical to closing or to an unaccepted proposed date.
  10. authorized instruction Turn 20. An authorized instruction identifies the buyer's actual decision; it is distinct from this preliminary exploration of options.

Dialogue in the book, page 46 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Thirty days remains a proposed completion date

The lesson's proposed offer seeks completion in thirty days, but the buyer's financing timeline is provisional.

  1. Buyer: I'd like completion in thirty days. Can we promise the seller that date?
  2. Buying agent: Your financing timeline is still provisional, so we cannot present that date as guaranteed.
  3. Buyer: Could a financing contingency make the timing certain regardless of when the lender finishes?
  4. Buying agent: We shouldn't assume that. Any proposed contingency and its implications need appropriate review.
  5. Buyer: What choices can we discuss now without presenting the financing as already settled?
  6. Buying agent: We can present thirty days as requested, with financing uncertainty explicit, or wait for the lender's timeline before proposing timing.
  7. Buyer: I'll choose to wait for the lender's timeline. Please don't communicate a firm completion commitment yet.
  8. Buying agent: Understood. Waiting gives us more timing information but delays presenting that part of the proposal.
  9. Buyer: I accept that tradeoff. I'll request the lender's estimate, without treating it as the seller's agreement.
  10. Buying agent: Then we'll review the timing and terms together. No completion date or seller acceptance is confirmed.
An appraisal gap is not an unlimited instruction

Separate fictional offer exercise: a buyer is willing to discuss an appraisal-gap provision but has given no amount or final instruction.

  1. Buying agent: You said you would discuss an appraisal-gap provision. What limit, if any, are you considering?
  2. Buyer: I haven't decided an amount. I didn't mean I would cover any possible difference.
  3. Buying agent: Then we should keep the discussion separate from an offer instruction or financial commitment.
  4. Buyer: Could we compare a capped proposal with leaving the issue for further negotiation?
  5. Buying agent: We can discuss those options, subject to your circumstances and review of the actual wording.
  6. Buyer: Would a proposed cap automatically tell us how the lender will respond?
  7. Buying agent: No. Financing implications need lender clarification; we shouldn't infer them from a conversational example.
  8. Buyer: Please request that clarification before presenting any figure on my behalf.
  9. Buying agent: I will. Your willingness to explore a term isn't authorization to submit an unlimited commitment.
  10. Buyer: Good. Let's agree the limit and review the conditions before changing the offer.
A backup offer does not replace the first agreement automatically

Separate fictional negotiation: a buyer wants to discuss a backup offer while another transaction is pending; no backup terms or acceptance are supplied.

  1. Buyer: If we make a backup offer, can we assume the property will become ours if the first buyer hesitates?
  2. Buying agent: No. We need to understand the actual status and review any proposed backup terms.
  3. Buyer: Then being a backup doesn't mean we control when the existing transaction ends.
  4. Buying agent: Correct. We shouldn't promise availability or invent how a condition operates without the relevant documents.
  5. Buyer: Could we ask about the process while keeping our own commitment undecided?
  6. Buying agent: Yes. I'll request the appropriate information and bring any proposed terms for your review.
  7. Buyer: I also want to compare the effect on pursuing other properties before giving instructions.
  8. Buying agent: That is a question for review, not something to resolve with a universal assurance.
  9. Buyer: Then our next step is an information request, not a submitted offer.
  10. Buying agent: Agreed. I'll preserve that boundary and avoid describing a backup position as secured.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

A thirty-day offer with an unconfirmed loan timeline
  1. After checking the key, read the offer discussion. Contrast a proposed thirty-day close with the lender's provisional thirty-five-to-forty-five-day range.
  2. Switch roles for the deposit and notice discussion. Keep $8,000, the exact contractual conditions, and the need for authorized instructions unchanged.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A request to extend is still pending

An inspection-response deadline in a fictional contract is Friday at 5 p.m. The buyer has asked to move it to Monday. No agreement to the change has been received.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Agent: "The proposed new deadline is ___."

Answer and explanation

C. Monday

Monday is the requested date, not an already accepted contractual change.

2. Buyer: "The existing stated deadline remains ___ at 5 p.m."

Answer and explanation

D. Friday

No accepted change is supplied, so the original stated deadline must not be treated as replaced.

3. Agent: "We need confirmation of the required ___."

Answer and explanation

C. agreement

The request alone does not establish that the other party has accepted the alteration.

4. Buyer: "Do not describe the extension as ___."

Answer and explanation

C. approved

The case supplies no approval, so that label would invent a completed decision.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Course: Real Estate English
Professional audience: real estate agents, brokers, transaction coordinators, property managers, leasing teams, and commercial real estate staff
Scope: Fictional English practice using mainly US real-estate terminology, not legal, lending, valuation, engineering, or safety advice. Agency, advertising, disclosure, lease, and closing requirements vary. Actual transactions require current documents, local rules, authorized instructions, and appropriately qualified professionals.
Lesson 05: Offers, Counteroffers, Negotiation, and Contingencies
Original fictional case: Buyer Tomas wants to propose a $420,000 purchase, an $8,000 earnest-money deposit, and closing in 30 days. The lender has given only a provisional 35-45-day processing estimate, not final approval. No offer has been submitted or accepted. Agent Elise must explain the timing mismatch and review the proposed financing contingency and deposit terms with the appropriate professionals. The buyer has not authorized removing any protection, and no seller concession or extension has been agreed.
Language workshop: A thirty-day offer with an unconfirmed loan timeline
Communication goal: Discuss offer timing and protections without turning a proposal or lender estimate into a binding assurance.
Language guidance: Proposed closing in 30 days is not the same as a lender confirming that financing can be ready then. An estimate of 35-45 days creates a specific issue to resolve. Avoid describing either the proposed date or the provisional estimate as a guarantee.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The proposed 30-day close is earlier than the lender's provisional range. / No offer has been submitted or accepted yet. / Let us ask the lender what supports the current timing estimate. / I will not remove a protection without your informed instruction and proper review. / We need to read the financing contingency's exact terms. / The deposit's treatment depends on the contract and applicable requirements. / Asking for an extension does not mean the seller has agreed. / Confirm the timing and terms before authorizing the offer. / Your proposed purchase price is $420,000. / The proposed earnest-money amount is $8,000. / Who must receive the notice, by what method, and by when? / Closing and possession dates should not be assumed identical. / Which terms are you authorizing us to propose? / Urgency does not remove the need to understand the consequences. / A counteroffer changes the proposed terms and requires a decision. / Use the exact version you have reviewed and authorized.
Vocabulary: purchase offer: Proposed terms for buying a property. / counteroffer: A response proposing different terms instead of accepting the original offer. / acceptance: Agreement to an offer under the applicable legal requirements. / offer expiration: The point when an offer ceases to remain open under its terms. / earnest money: A deposit showing commitment, governed by the contract and applicable rules. / deposit holder: The authorized person or entity holding a transaction deposit. / contingency: A contractual condition affecting obligations or available rights. / financing contingency: A contract condition addressing financing under specified terms. / inspection contingency: A contract condition addressing inspection and related rights. / appraisal contingency: A contract condition addressing appraised value and related rights. / home-sale contingency: A condition connected to selling another property. / contingency deadline: The contractual time limit for a condition or related action. / waiver: Giving up a right or condition under applicable requirements. / amendment: An agreed change to an existing agreement. / addendum: Additional document or terms incorporated into an agreement. / seller credit: A seller contribution toward specified buyer costs under permitted terms. / possession date: The date the buyer is entitled to take possession under the agreement. / closing date: The scheduled or agreed date for completing closing steps. / extension request: A proposal to move an existing deadline. / notice requirement: Rules governing how and when a contractual notice must be given. / default: Failure to meet a contractual obligation as defined by the agreement and law. / remedy: A response or relief available under an agreement or law. / authorized instruction: A direction given by someone with the relevant decision-making authority. / negotiating position: The terms and priorities a party is prepared to advance.
Speaking task: After checking the key, read the offer discussion. Contrast a proposed thirty-day close with the lender's provisional thirty-five-to-forty-five-day range. Switch roles for the deposit and notice discussion. Keep $8,000, the exact contractual conditions, and the need for authorized instructions unchanged. Complete the extension exchange and check its key. Read Friday at five as the existing deadline and Monday as the requested, unconfirmed change.
Partner: Tomas: Buyer / Elise: Buyer's agent
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: An inspection-response deadline in a fictional contract is Friday at 5 p.m. The buyer has asked to move it to Monday. No agreement to the change has been received.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Tomas: The possession date matters as well because I need to arrange a move. I should not book everything just from the proposed closing line.
Elise: Right. The possession date must be checked separately in the terms. We should not promise access to the property before the relevant agreement and closing conditions are confirmed.
Tomas: Ask the lender about a realistic date first. Then walk me through the conditions before I authorize the exact offer you will submit.
Elise: I will record your authorized instruction after that review and confirm the exact version before submission. At present we have a proposal to examine, not an accepted contract or a guaranteed timeline.
END REFERENCE

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

06Inspections, Repairs, Disclosures, and Due DiligenceAn inspection finding is not a repair diagnosis+

Your goal

Relay a technical finding accurately, arrange further evaluation, and distinguish a repair request from an agreement.

This lesson in the book, page 49 ↗

A Read the situation

An inspection finding is not a repair diagnosis

A home inspection reports staining on a basement wall and recommends evaluation by a qualified moisture specialist. It does not establish the cause, give a repair design, or estimate a repair cost. The seller's disclosure marks prior water intrusion as unknown. Buyer Nina asks agent Omar whether the wall only needs paint and whether the seller must pay. No specialist appointment or repair agreement is confirmed. The contractual inspection-response requirements need review before any decision or deadline assurance.

Nina: Buyer / Omar: Buyer's agent

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What does the report establish in this case?

Answer and explanation

B. Staining was observed and specialist evaluation was recommended

The report states an observation and recommendation, not a cause, repair specification, or contractual agreement.

2. How does the seller's disclosure describe prior water intrusion?

Answer and explanation

A. Unknown

Unknown records an unresolved fact; it is not proof of absence, repair, or an agreed concession.

3. Which next step is supported?

Answer and explanation

A. Arrange qualified evaluation and review the contractual response requirements

The case needs technical evaluation and contract review before a diagnosis, cost, or obligation can be asserted.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Observed staining, suspected cause, and confirmed diagnosis are different levels of information. The supplied report recommends a specialist; it does not say paint is sufficient. A seller's unknown response is also not a representation that water intrusion never occurred.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
home inspection
An assessment of a property's condition within a defined professional scope.arrange a home inspection
inspection scope
The systems, access, and services covered by an inspection.review the inspection scope
visual observation
A condition identified through what can be seen.record a visual observation
accessible component
A component available for inspection under the stated access limits.identify accessible components
inspection limitation
A condition restricting what could be inspected or concluded.document an inspection limitation
deficiency
An observed shortcoming or condition requiring attention in context.describe the reported deficiency
further evaluation
Additional assessment by an appropriately qualified professional.recommend further evaluation
specialist referral
Direction to someone with relevant expertise for a specific issue.coordinate a specialist referral
moisture intrusion
Entry of water or moisture into a building area.investigate moisture intrusion
staining
Visible discoloration that may need explanation or evaluation.document wall staining
root cause
The underlying source of an identified problem.establish the root cause
repair scope
The work specified to address a condition.define the repair scope
repair estimate
An approximate price for specified repair work.obtain a repair estimate
contractor quotation
A contractor's priced proposal for a stated scope and conditions.review the contractor quotation
permit
Official authorization for work where required.verify permit requirements
code compliance
Conformity with applicable building requirements.obtain qualified code-compliance review
reinspection
A subsequent inspection to assess specified work or conditions.arrange a reinspection
warranty
A defined promise concerning performance, repair, or other coverage.review warranty exclusions
seller disclosure
Information about a property supplied by the seller under applicable requirements.review the seller disclosure
disclosure supplement
Additional information added to an earlier disclosure.request a disclosure supplement
due diligence
The investigation and review undertaken before a transaction decision.track due-diligence items
repair request
A proposal asking another party to undertake specified work.submit a repair request
repair agreement
Accepted terms governing specified repair work.confirm the repair agreement
repair credit
A negotiated financial allowance instead of or toward repair work.review the proposed repair credit

A referral is not a confirmed appointment, an estimate is not an agreed price for every possible repair, and a repair request is not an accepted obligation. Keep the technical assessment and contractual decision moving together without pretending either is finished.

C Notice the language

Be useful without borrowing another profession's certainty

An agent can locate the relevant report passage, coordinate a referral, and track the contractual steps. That is substantive help. Avoid turning a request for reassurance into a technical diagnosis, a guarantee of safety, or a conclusion about another party's obligations.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Attribute the finding
The report records staining and recommends specialist evaluation.
Limit the diagnosis
It does not establish the cause or a repair design.
Correct the assumption
We cannot conclude that paint alone will resolve it.
Explain unknown
The seller marked that history as unknown, not confirmed absent.
Coordinate expertise
I can help arrange an appropriately qualified specialist.
Keep the cost open
No repair scope or reliable cost has been established.
Separate the request
Asking the seller to act is not the same as an agreement.
Close with tracking
We will track the evaluation and contractual response requirements.
Check the scope
What did the inspection cover, and what was inaccessible?
Request the wording
Let us read the exact report passage together.
Avoid a guarantee
I cannot certify the condition from this description.
Verify the appointment
A referral has been sent; the visit is not yet confirmed.
Clarify the quote
Does this price cover evaluation or the specified repair work?
Check completion
We need appropriate evidence that any agreed work was completed.
Review the deadline
Confirm the contract's dates, notice method, and available options.
Preserve the record
Keep the report, responses, and any agreed changes together.
6 language and precision notes
Records versus diagnoses
A report can document a visible condition without identifying its cause.
Unknown versus no
Unknown does not establish the negative fact that something never happened.
Recommended versus arranged
A recommendation does not prove that an appointment has been booked.
Estimate for what
A price needs a specified service or repair scope.
Must pay
This asserts an obligation and needs contractual or legal support, not an agent's reassurance.
Resolved
Reserve this for an adequately verified outcome, not a sent message or referral.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which handover to the specialist preserves exactly what the report establishes?

Answer and explanation

D. Basement staining observed; cause and repair scope not established.

The report documents staining and recommends further evaluation. It supplies no cause, repair history, active plumbing diagnosis, or warranty finding.

2. How should the unknown disclosure response be interpreted?

Answer and explanation

B. The relevant history is not established by that answer.

Unknown does not establish either absence, completed repair, compliance, or a contractual concession.

3. Which statement about seller payment is appropriate?

Answer and explanation

A. We need the actual contract and any negotiated agreement before asserting an obligation.

The case supplies no agreement or established obligation, so the contractual question requires review.

4. Which update correctly distinguishes progress?

Answer and explanation

A. The referral is underway; the appointment and repair scope remain unconfirmed.

The update reports only the actual referral step and leaves unfinished arrangements and terms open.

Check explanations in the book, page 95 ↗

E Conversations

An inspection finding is not a repair diagnosis

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Nina: Buyer / Omar: Buyer's agent

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank

  1. Nina
    The report shows staining on the basement wall. Can we assume it only needs paint, or does the photograph tell you what caused it?
  2. Omar
    The 1 is staining. The report does not establish the cause, and I should not turn a photograph into a diagnosis or tell you that paint will resolve it.
  3. Nina
    The inspector recommends a moisture specialist. I was hoping the general inspection would answer every question before I had to contact anyone else.
  4. Omar
    We should review the 2 and the exact recommendation. An inspection can identify an issue requiring another professional's assessment without supplying that specialist analysis itself.
  5. Nina
    I noticed that the seller marked previous water intrusion as unknown. Is that effectively the same as saying there has never been a problem?
  6. Omar
    No. The 3 leaves that history unresolved. We should preserve the word unknown instead of paraphrasing it as a confident no.
  7. Nina
    Who should look at this next, and can you help arrange it? I need to know what to do before the response deadline.
  8. Omar
    I can help coordinate a 4 and track the response. We will ask about the relevant qualifications, availability, and evaluation scope before describing any visit as confirmed.
  9. Nina
    Once the specialist looks at it, I want to understand why the staining occurred, not just receive a general suggestion to cover the mark.
  10. Omar
    That is a question about the 5. The qualified evaluator can explain their findings and limits. I can help organize the information, but I cannot supply that technical conclusion in advance.
  11. Nina
    If work is needed, I would also want the proposal to say exactly what is included. A single unexplained number would not be enough.
  12. Omar
    Ask for the 6 and its conditions. Evaluation, repair, permits where required, and follow-up checks may be different items rather than one automatic package.
  13. Nina
    Could we ask the seller to handle the work? I do not want your answer to imply that they have already accepted responsibility.
  14. Omar
    We can discuss a 7 after the relevant review. A request is not a repair agreement, and the actual contract and applicable rules determine the available process.
  15. Nina
    Timing worries me. If arranging the specialist takes longer than expected, does that automatically extend the inspection-response deadline?
  16. Omar
    No. We need to track the 8 alongside the contract requirements. Any extension or notice needs the proper process, rather than an assumption that the clock stops during evaluation.
  17. Nina
    If the seller eventually agrees to work, how would I know that the agreed scope was actually completed before relying on it?
  18. Omar
    The agreement should address suitable completion evidence and any appropriate 9. We should not call the matter resolved solely because someone says a contractor has been contacted.
  19. Nina
    Please pursue the specialist visit and check the deadline at the same time. I do not want to lose time while we wait for an appointment.
  20. Omar
    Exactly. Any proposed 10 or work agreement will need its own review and acceptance. I will give you a status update that separates each completed step from what remains open.

Answers and explanations
  1. visual observation Turn 2. The observation identifies visible staining; it does not establish the underlying cause or the work needed to address it.
  2. inspection scope Turn 4. Inspection scope identifies what the inspection covers and its limits; a general report need not resolve every specialist question.
  3. seller disclosure Turn 6. The seller disclosure records an unknown history here, not a verified statement that water intrusion never occurred.
  4. specialist referral Turn 8. A specialist referral connects the buyer with appropriate expertise; it does not itself establish a diagnosis or confirmed appointment.
  5. root cause Turn 10. The root cause is the underlying source of the problem, which the present inspection has not identified.
  6. repair scope Turn 12. Repair scope defines the actual work being priced; without it, a cost figure may refer to a different or incomplete service.
  7. repair request Turn 14. A repair request proposes work for negotiation; the seller has not yet accepted any repair obligation in the case.
  8. due diligence Turn 16. Due diligence includes the investigation and contractual review; continuing an evaluation does not itself alter a contractual deadline.
  9. reinspection Turn 18. A reinspection can assess specified completed work or conditions; it is distinct from merely receiving a contractor's promise.
  10. repair credit Turn 20. A repair credit is a negotiated allowance; the current report does not establish its amount or the seller's acceptance.

Dialogue in the book, page 55 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

An inspection observation is not the agent's diagnosis

The lesson's inspection report identifies an issue and recommends specialist evaluation; its cause and repair scope are not supplied.

  1. Buyer: The inspection report flags an issue. Can you tell me exactly what's causing it?
  2. Real estate agent: The report recommends specialist evaluation. I can explain that next step, but not diagnose the issue.
  3. Buyer: So the observed issue and the cause are different levels of information here.
  4. Real estate agent: Exactly. We shouldn't turn a recommendation for evaluation into a confirmed repair diagnosis.
  5. Buyer: Could you estimate the concession we should request before the specialist checks it?
  6. Real estate agent: No repair scope or cost is supplied. We need relevant information before discussing a supported proposal.
  7. Buyer: Does the inspection period tell us which timing questions we should ask the transaction team?
  8. Real estate agent: Yes, using the actual agreement and appropriate review, not a deadline invented in this conversation.
  9. Buyer: Please help arrange the specialist inquiry and keep the cause unresolved in our discussion.
  10. Real estate agent: I will. We'll distinguish the report's observation, evaluation recommendation, and any later findings.
A credit is not evidence of completed repair

Separate fictional due-diligence conversation: the seller proposes a repair credit, but no repair completion evidence is supplied.

  1. Buyer: The seller offered a credit. Does that mean the defect will be repaired before we proceed?
  2. Buying agent: A proposed financial concession isn't evidence that repair work has been completed or even agreed.
  3. Buyer: Then the credit proposal and the physical condition need to be discussed separately.
  4. Buying agent: Correct. We need the actual terms and any specialist information about the work.
  5. Buyer: Could the amount itself prove the repair will be adequate?
  6. Buying agent: No. A number doesn't establish scope, quality, or completion, and we don't have those findings.
  7. Buyer: I'd like to understand the issue before treating the concession as a full solution.
  8. Buying agent: I'll request the relevant information and arrange review of the proposal's conditions.
  9. Buyer: Please don't tell the transaction team that the repair concern is resolved yet.
  10. Buying agent: Agreed. The current status is a proposed concession with the underlying assessment still open.
A disclosure form is not a test result

Separate fictional property review: a file contains a lead-based paint disclosure document, but no test result is supplied. Applicable requirements are not being determined in this exercise.

  1. Buyer: The file includes a lead-based paint disclosure. Does that prove the property tested clear?
  2. Transaction agent: No test result is supplied here. A disclosure document and a testing result are different records.
  3. Buyer: So I shouldn't interpret the document's title as a finding about the property's condition.
  4. Transaction agent: Correct. We should examine what the document actually states and identify any missing assessment.
  5. Buyer: Can you tell me what inspection or legal requirement applies from this short description alone?
  6. Transaction agent: No. Those questions need the actual property facts, relevant documents, and qualified current review.
  7. Buyer: Please help me ask the appropriate professional what information is available and what remains unknown.
  8. Transaction agent: I will, without describing the absence of a supplied result as either safety confirmation or confirmed contamination.
  9. Buyer: That distinction helps me understand the paperwork without assuming a diagnosis.
  10. Transaction agent: Good. We'll keep the document, any testing evidence, and applicable requirements separate during review.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

An inspection finding is not a repair diagnosis
  1. Check the key, then read the inspection discussion. Stress observed staining, unknown history, and specialist evaluation without adding a diagnosis.
  2. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Distinguish scope, request, agreement, and completion evidence; preserve the need to check the response deadline.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

The quotation covers evaluation only

A specialist quotes $250 for an assessment visit. The quotation excludes repairs. The visit is not yet booked, and no repair design or price has been supplied.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Buyer: "The $250 is for the ___."

Answer and explanation

C. assessment

The supplied quotation prices an evaluation visit rather than repair work.

2. Agent: "It excludes ___."

Answer and explanation

B. repairs

The quotation expressly excludes repairs, so they must not be described as included.

3. Buyer: "The appointment still needs ___."

Answer and explanation

D. confirmation

The visit has not been booked, so the quotation is not evidence of a confirmed appointment.

4. Agent: "A repair price will need a defined ___."

Answer and explanation

C. scope

A meaningful repair price requires specified work, which has not yet been supplied.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Lesson 06: Inspections, Repairs, Disclosures, and Due Diligence
Original fictional case: A home inspection reports staining on a basement wall and recommends evaluation by a qualified moisture specialist. It does not establish the cause, give a repair design, or estimate a repair cost. The seller's disclosure marks prior water intrusion as unknown. Buyer Nina asks agent Omar whether the wall only needs paint and whether the seller must pay. No specialist appointment or repair agreement is confirmed. The contractual inspection-response requirements need review before any decision or deadline assurance.
Language workshop: An inspection finding is not a repair diagnosis
Communication goal: Relay a technical finding accurately, arrange further evaluation, and distinguish a repair request from an agreement.
Language guidance: Observed staining, suspected cause, and confirmed diagnosis are different levels of information. The supplied report recommends a specialist; it does not say paint is sufficient. A seller's unknown response is also not a representation that water intrusion never occurred.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The report records staining and recommends specialist evaluation. / It does not establish the cause or a repair design. / We cannot conclude that paint alone will resolve it. / The seller marked that history as unknown, not confirmed absent. / I can help arrange an appropriately qualified specialist. / No repair scope or reliable cost has been established. / Asking the seller to act is not the same as an agreement. / We will track the evaluation and contractual response requirements. / What did the inspection cover, and what was inaccessible? / Let us read the exact report passage together. / I cannot certify the condition from this description. / A referral has been sent; the visit is not yet confirmed. / Does this price cover evaluation or the specified repair work? / We need appropriate evidence that any agreed work was completed. / Confirm the contract's dates, notice method, and available options. / Keep the report, responses, and any agreed changes together.
Vocabulary: home inspection: An assessment of a property's condition within a defined professional scope. / inspection scope: The systems, access, and services covered by an inspection. / visual observation: A condition identified through what can be seen. / accessible component: A component available for inspection under the stated access limits. / inspection limitation: A condition restricting what could be inspected or concluded. / deficiency: An observed shortcoming or condition requiring attention in context. / further evaluation: Additional assessment by an appropriately qualified professional. / specialist referral: Direction to someone with relevant expertise for a specific issue. / moisture intrusion: Entry of water or moisture into a building area. / staining: Visible discoloration that may need explanation or evaluation. / root cause: The underlying source of an identified problem. / repair scope: The work specified to address a condition. / repair estimate: An approximate price for specified repair work. / contractor quotation: A contractor's priced proposal for a stated scope and conditions. / permit: Official authorization for work where required. / code compliance: Conformity with applicable building requirements. / reinspection: A subsequent inspection to assess specified work or conditions. / warranty: A defined promise concerning performance, repair, or other coverage. / seller disclosure: Information about a property supplied by the seller under applicable requirements. / disclosure supplement: Additional information added to an earlier disclosure. / due diligence: The investigation and review undertaken before a transaction decision. / repair request: A proposal asking another party to undertake specified work. / repair agreement: Accepted terms governing specified repair work. / repair credit: A negotiated financial allowance instead of or toward repair work.
Speaking task: Check the key, then read the inspection discussion. Stress observed staining, unknown history, and specialist evaluation without adding a diagnosis. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Distinguish scope, request, agreement, and completion evidence; preserve the need to check the response deadline. Complete and check the quotation exchange. Read $250 as assessment only, with repairs excluded and the appointment still unconfirmed.
Partner: Nina: Buyer / Omar: Buyer's agent
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A specialist quotes $250 for an assessment visit. The quotation excludes repairs. The visit is not yet booked, and no repair design or price has been supplied.

Omar: The agreement should address suitable completion evidence and any appropriate reinspection. We should not call the matter resolved solely because someone says a contractor has been contacted.
Nina: Please pursue the specialist visit and check the deadline at the same time. I do not want to lose time while we wait for an appointment.
Omar: Exactly. Any proposed repair credit or work agreement will need its own review and acceptance. I will give you a status update that separates each completed step from what remains open.
END REFERENCE

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.
