REFERENCE
Course: Real Estate English
Professional audience: real estate agents, brokers, transaction coordinators, property managers, leasing teams, and commercial real estate staff
Scope: Fictional English practice using mainly US real-estate terminology, not legal, lending, valuation, engineering, or safety advice. Agency, advertising, disclosure, lease, and closing requirements vary. Actual transactions require current documents, local rules, authorized instructions, and appropriately qualified professionals.
Dialogue 01: Buyer Consultation: Agreement Before Touring
Original fictional setting: A buyer wants to see a house immediately but has not discussed representation or compensation.
Professional roles: Buyer / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Buyer: Can you show me the house this afternoon? I do not want to sign anything yet.
Agent: Before arranging representation and a tour, let's review the applicable law, brokerage policy, and any agreement requirements. I will explain the services, term, and compensation arrangements clearly.
Transaction adviser: This agreement is not meant to pressure you. It defines who I represent, what I can do for you, and what compensation we agree to. We can keep the term narrow if you only want to evaluate this property.
Buyer: So I have to pay you?
Transaction adviser: Compensation is negotiable and may be paid in different ways depending on the offer and transaction. The important point is that we discuss it clearly before we start representation.
Buyer: I will review the proposed services and ask about anything unclear.
Transaction adviser: We can document the arrangement only after the relevant terms and requirements are understood.
END REFERENCE

Course: Real Estate English
Professional audience: real estate agents, brokers, transaction coordinators, property managers, leasing teams, and commercial real estate staff

Dialogue 02: Fair Housing Question: 'Is This a Good Neighborhood?'
Original fictional setting: A buyer asks for subjective neighborhood advice that could lead to steering.
Professional roles: Buyer / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Buyer: Is this a good neighborhood for families like us?
Agent: I can help you compare objective information, but I cannot steer you based on who lives here.
Transaction adviser: Let's define what 'good' means for you: commute time, budget, property condition, parks, school district boundaries, noise, transit, or walkability. I can point you to public resources so you can evaluate the area using your own priorities.
Buyer: But would you live here?
Transaction adviser: I should not substitute my personal preference for your decision. I can give you property facts and objective sources, and you can decide whether the area fits your needs.
Buyer: I will compare the objective information against the buyer's stated priorities.
Transaction adviser: Keep the discussion focused on property facts and the buyer's own criteria.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 03: Listing Presentation: Seller Wants an Unrealistic Price
Original fictional setting: A seller wants to list far above the CMA range because a neighbor got a high price last year.
Professional roles: Seller / Listing agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Seller: My neighbor sold for more last year. I want to list at that number plus 10 percent.
Listing agent: The market has changed since then.
Transaction adviser: We can test a premium only if the evidence supports it. The closest recent comps show lower closed prices, longer DOM, and seller concessions. If we list too high, we may reduce urgency and help competing listings look more attractive.
Seller: I do not want to leave money on the table.
Transaction adviser: Neither do I. My recommendation is a price that creates serious buyer activity and gives us leverage. We can also agree now on a review point if showings or feedback are weak.
Seller: I will prepare the comparable-sales evidence and a proposed review point.
Transaction adviser: Make the assumptions and market dates clear in the pricing discussion.
Vocabulary in this exchange: DOM: Days on market; how long a property has been publicly listed under local rules.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 03: Listing Presentation: Seller Wants an Unrealistic Price
Original fictional setting: A seller wants to list far above the CMA range because a neighbor got a high price last year.
Professional roles: Seller / Listing agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Seller: My neighbor sold for more last year. I want to list at that number plus 10 percent.
Listing agent: The market has changed since then.
Transaction adviser: We can test a premium only if the evidence supports it. The closest recent comps show lower closed prices, longer DOM, and seller concessions. If we list too high, we may reduce urgency and help competing listings look more attractive.
Seller: I do not want to leave money on the table.
Transaction adviser: Neither do I. My recommendation is a price that creates serious buyer activity and gives us leverage. We can also agree now on a review point if showings or feedback are weak.
Seller: I will prepare the comparable-sales evidence and a proposed review point.
Transaction adviser: Make the assumptions and market dates clear in the pricing discussion.
Vocabulary in this exchange: DOM: Days on market; how long a property has been publicly listed under local rules.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 04: Multiple Offers: Stronger Terms vs Higher Price
Original fictional setting: A buyer wants to win in a competitive situation but does not understand the risk of waiving protections.
Professional roles: Buyer / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Buyer: Let's waive everything and offer over asking.
Agent: That may strengthen the offer, but it changes your risk.
Transaction adviser: We should compare price, appraisal gap, inspection rights, financing contingency, earnest money, closing date, and seller priorities. A stronger offer is not just a higher price. It is also certainty and clean terms.
Buyer: Can we waive inspection?
Transaction adviser: Waiving or changing inspection protections can have significant consequences. Let's review the actual contract, applicable local requirements, and qualified advice before you choose or authorize any strategy.
Buyer: I will ask for a comparison of the actual contractual options.
Transaction adviser: We will coordinate qualified review before you authorize any change to protections.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Appraisal: Independent opinion of value often required by a lender. / Earnest money: Deposit showing buyer seriousness, handled according to contract and escrow rules. / Contingency: Contract condition that must be satisfied or waived for the transaction to continue. / Appraisal gap: Difference between contract price and appraised value that can create financing or negotiation issues.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 05: Inspection Negotiation: Repair Credit
Original fictional setting: An inspection found roof and electrical issues. The buyer is angry and wants the seller to fix everything.
Professional roles: Buyer / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Buyer: This house has problems. Ask them to fix every item.
Agent: We need to separate major issues from normal maintenance.
Transaction adviser: The strongest request will focus on safety, systems, and cost. Instead of sending a long emotional list, we can ask for a licensed electrician to address the panel issue and request a credit toward the roof repair, supported by the inspection report and estimate.
Buyer: What if they refuse?
Transaction adviser: Then we evaluate your contract options, your appetite for repairs, and whether a revised price or credit makes the risk acceptable.
Buyer: I will gather the inspection references and estimates.
Transaction adviser: Then we can frame a specific request and review the available contractual options.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 06: Low Appraisal: Contract Price Is Higher Than Appraised Value
Original fictional setting: The appraisal comes in below contract price and financing is affected.
Professional roles: Lender / Buyer / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Lender: The appraisal is twenty thousand below contract price.
Buyer: Does that mean the deal is dead?
Transaction adviser: Not automatically. We have several paths: challenge the appraisal if there are factual issues, renegotiate price, increase down payment, use an appraisal-gap clause if one exists, or cancel if the contract allows it.
Buyer: What should we do?
Transaction adviser: First, let's review the appraisal with the lender and compare it to our comps. Then we can choose a negotiation position based on your cash, contract rights, and risk tolerance.
Lender: I will ask the lender to explain the appraisal implications.
Transaction adviser: We will assess the options against the actual contract and your verified resources.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Appraisal: Independent opinion of value often required by a lender.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 07: Financing Delay: Underwriting Conditions
Original fictional setting: Closing is approaching but the lender still needs documentation.
Professional roles: Seller agent / Buyer agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Seller agent: Are your buyers clear to close? We need certainty.
Buyer agent: The file is still in underwriting.
Transaction adviser: The lender has issued conditional approval and is waiting on two documents from the buyer. We expect an update tomorrow afternoon. I do not want to overpromise, so I will send a written status update by 4 p.m. with any impact on closing.
Seller agent: Should we issue a notice?
Transaction adviser: I understand your concern. Please send any contract notice through the proper channel. Meanwhile, I will keep the timeline, owner, and dependency clear for everyone.
Seller agent: I will track the outstanding documents with the lender.
Transaction adviser: Keep every party informed of confirmed changes through the proper transaction channels.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Underwriting: Lender review of borrower, property, income, assets, credit, and loan risk. / Clear to close: Lender status indicating conditions are substantially satisfied for closing.
END REFERENCE

Course: Real Estate English

Dialogue 08: RESPA Risk: Referral Benefit
Original fictional setting: A settlement-service provider offers valuable benefits for referrals.
Professional roles: Vendor / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Vendor: If you send us your buyers, we can sponsor your client event and give you premium tickets.
Agent: That sounds generous, but we need to be careful.
Transaction adviser: I cannot agree to benefits tied to settlement-service referrals. Any proposed arrangement needs broker and compliance review under the applicable rules and our policy before we discuss acceptance.
Vendor: Everyone does it.
Transaction adviser: Our policy is to protect clients and avoid referral-kickback risk. I can share your public information with clients if they ask for options, but I cannot trade referrals for benefits.
Vendor: I will send any proposed arrangement to the broker for review.
Transaction adviser: Keep acceptance pending and do not link any benefit to referrals.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Client: A person represented by the real estate professional under an agency or representation relationship.
END REFERENCE

Course: Real Estate English

Dialogue 09: Seller Disclosure: Known Water Intrusion
Original fictional setting: A seller wants to avoid disclosing a past water problem because it was repaired.
Professional roles: Seller / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Seller: Do we really need to mention the basement leak? It was fixed two years ago.
Agent: Known property issues can create disclosure duties.
Transaction adviser: I cannot tell you how to complete the legal disclosure form, but I can tell you not to hide known facts. Let's review the form instructions, gather repair records, and if you are unsure, ask your attorney before we publish or respond to buyers.
Seller: I am afraid buyers will panic.
Transaction adviser: Clear disclosure with documentation can reduce surprises later. A hidden issue can create a much larger trust and contract problem.
Seller: I will assemble the repair records and form instructions.
Transaction adviser: Qualified advice can resolve the disclosure questions before the response is finalized.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 10: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure
Original fictional setting: A pre-1978 home is going under contract and documents are incomplete.
Professional roles: Transaction coordinator / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Transaction coordinator: The lead disclosure form is missing the buyer acknowledgment.
Agent: Can we just send it after signatures?
Transaction adviser: We need to check the applicable lead-disclosure requirements, including whether this property and transaction are covered and when the required steps must occur. Route the incomplete file to the responsible broker or compliance reviewer before proceeding.
Agent: The seller does not know of any lead paint.
Transaction adviser: A lack of known lead information does not by itself resolve the disclosure question. Let's verify the applicable forms, information, timing, acknowledgments, and any inspection-related requirements with the authorized reviewer.
Transaction coordinator: I will flag the incomplete item in the transaction checklist.
Transaction adviser: The responsible reviewer should confirm the applicable steps before the file proceeds.
END REFERENCE

Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Course: Real Estate English
Professional audience: real estate agents, brokers, transaction coordinators, property managers, leasing teams, and commercial real estate staff
Scope: Fictional English practice using mainly US real-estate terminology, not legal, lending, valuation, engineering, or safety advice. Agency, advertising, disclosure, lease, and closing requirements vary. Actual transactions require current documents, local rules, authorized instructions, and appropriately qualified professionals.
Dialogue 11: Dual Agency or Same-Brokerage Conflict
Original fictional setting: A buyer wants to make an offer on a listing held by the same brokerage.
Professional roles: Buyer / Agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Buyer: Can you still represent me if your office has the listing?
Agent: It depends on state law, brokerage policy, and the agency structure.
Transaction adviser: We need to disclose the relationship clearly and explain whether this is dual agency, designated agency, or another permitted arrangement. You should understand what advice I can and cannot give before you decide whether to consent.
Buyer: Will you tell me what the seller will accept?
Transaction adviser: I cannot share confidential information from another client or side. My role and limits must be clear before we proceed.
Buyer: I will request a clear explanation of the permitted representation structure.
Transaction adviser: Document the required disclosures and decisions through the applicable process.
Vocabulary in this exchange: Client: A person represented by the real estate professional under an agency or representation relationship. / Dual agency: Representation of both buyer and seller in the same transaction where allowed and properly disclosed. / Designated agency: Same brokerage but different designated agents represent different clients, where permitted.
END REFERENCE

Course: Real Estate English
Professional audience: real estate agents, brokers, transaction coordinators, property managers, leasing teams, and commercial real estate staff
Scope: Fictional English practice using mainly US real-estate terminology, not legal, lending, valuation, engineering, or safety advice. Agency, advertising, disclosure, lease, and closing requirements vary. Actual transactions require current documents, local rules, authorized instructions, and appropriately qualified professionals.
Dialogue 12: Commercial Lease: NNN and TI Allowance
Original fictional setting: A small business owner is reviewing a commercial lease proposal.
Professional roles: Tenant / Commercial agent / Transaction adviser
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Tenant: The rent looks affordable. It says NNN, CAM, and TI allowance. What does that mean?
Commercial agent: Those terms affect your real occupancy cost.
Transaction adviser: Base rent is only one part. NNN usually means you may pay taxes, insurance, and maintenance in addition to base rent. CAM covers common area maintenance. A TI allowance is landlord contribution toward tenant improvements, but the lease will define conditions and repayment risk.
Tenant: So can I sign the LOI?
Transaction adviser: An LOI can frame the deal, but you should review lease language with legal and financial advisors before committing. Let's compare total occupancy cost, term, options, buildout timeline, and exit risk.
Tenant: I will prepare a total-occupancy-cost comparison using the draft lease.
Transaction adviser: Flag assumptions and obtain the appropriate legal and financial review before commitment.
Vocabulary in this exchange: CAM: Common area maintenance charges in some commercial leases. / NNN: Triple net lease structure where tenant may pay taxes, insurance, and maintenance in addition to base rent.
END REFERENCE

REFERENCE
Course: Real Estate English
Professional audience: real estate agents, brokers, transaction coordinators, property managers, leasing teams, and commercial real estate staff
Scope: Fictional English practice using mainly US real-estate terminology, not legal, lending, valuation, engineering, or safety advice. Agency, advertising, disclosure, lease, and closing requirements vary. Actual transactions require current documents, local rules, authorized instructions, and appropriately qualified professionals.
Lesson 01: Agency, Representation, Compensation, and Trust
Original fictional case: Prospective buyer Lena asks licensee Ren whether Ren represents both sides of a property transaction. Their relationship has not been established or documented, and the brokerage role for the particular listing still needs confirmation. No fee terms have been agreed. Lena is about to disclose her maximum offer. Ren can explain the questions that must be settled and obtain the applicable documents and broker guidance, but must not promise unrestricted advocacy, a standard commission, or confidentiality beyond the actual relationship and applicable duties.
Language workshop: Before the buyer shares a negotiating limit
Communication goal: Clarify representation, confidentiality, and compensation without assuming an agreement already exists.
Language guidance: Providing access or information does not, by itself, explain whom a licensee represents. Ask for the actual relationship and its duties. Labels such as dual agency or transaction broker cannot be assumed available or identical across jurisdictions.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): We should clarify whom the brokerage represents before discussing your strategy. / Please hold your maximum offer until we have clarified the relationship. / I need to confirm the brokerage's role for this listing. / Let us review the applicable agreement and disclosures. / The representation role and fee obligations are distinct questions. / Available arrangements and duties depend on the applicable rules. / We can explain the proposed terms before you decide whether to agree. / I will obtain the role information and broker guidance first. / The agreement should identify the services included. / What dates and properties does this term cover? / Let us check what the exclusivity provision actually restricts. / No compensation terms have been agreed in this conversation. / The documents need to explain who owes which payment under what conditions. / I cannot promise duties beyond the actual relationship and applicable requirements. / Which part of the proposed arrangement would you like clarified? / Does this explanation distinguish representation from payment?
Vocabulary: agency: A legal representation relationship defined by applicable law. / principal: The person or entity represented by an agent. / fiduciary duty: A duty of loyalty or care arising in a relationship under applicable law. / buyer representation: Acting for a buyer under an established relationship. / seller representation: Acting for a seller under an established relationship. / dual agency: Representation of both sides where permitted and subject to applicable conditions. / designated agency: An arrangement assigning different representatives within a brokerage where permitted. / non-agency relationship: A permitted service relationship without an agency role. / transaction broker: A professional facilitating a transaction under a jurisdiction's non-agency framework. / brokerage: The business through which real-estate services are provided. / managing broker: The broker responsible for supervision under the relevant structure. / representation agreement: A document setting out a representation relationship and terms. / listing agreement: An agreement for marketing or representing a property's seller. / exclusivity: A contractual restriction on using other representatives within a stated scope. / agreement term: The period during which an agreement operates. / service scope: The work included in the professional engagement. / compensation: Payment for professional services on agreed terms. / commission: A form of compensation often linked to a completed transaction. / fee obligation: A contractual responsibility to pay a specified fee. / informed consent: Agreement based on relevant information and understanding. / conflict of interest: A competing interest that may affect professional judgment or duties. / confidential information: Information subject to protection under applicable duties or terms. / material fact: A fact important to a transaction or decision in context. / termination provision: Terms governing how an agreement may end.
Speaking task: Check the cloze key, then read Lena and Ren's exchange. Pause before Lena's maximum-offer question; stress Ren's words that leave the relationship unresolved. Switch roles and reread turns 9-20. Keep service scope, exclusivity, compensation, and termination as separate questions; do not invent agreed terms. Complete the shorter agreement exchange and check its key. Read it with the proposed shorter term still unsigned and unaccepted.
Partner: Lena: Prospective buyer / Ren: Real-estate licensee
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A prospective seller receives a proposed service package and fee. They ask for a shorter term. The brokerage has not accepted the change, and the proposal is unsigned.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Lena: I would like time to read the terms, including when the agreement ends and what would happen if I wanted to stop working together.
Ren: We should review the termination provision as well as the duration. I can explain the proposal within my role and direct legal-interpretation questions to qualified counsel when needed.
Lena: Please send the proposed terms and confirm your office's role. I will wait to discuss my maximum offer until those questions are answered.
Ren: Correct. Any required informed consent must follow a clear explanation of the actual arrangement. Today I will obtain the missing information, not promise unrestricted advocacy before the relationship is settled.
END REFERENCE
